summary:
Same-sex conduct is not a criminal offence in Belize. On 10 August 2016 the Supreme Court, presided over by Chief Justice Kenneth Benjamin, declared the colonial-era Section 53 sodomy law unconstitutional in the case brought by LGBT advocate Caleb Orozco, filed in 2010 and heard in Belize City in May 2013. On 30 December 2019 the Appeals Court upheld that decision and confirmed that the Constitution's protections against discrimination extend to sexual orientation and that freedom of expression includes sexual expression. Belize was the first former British Caribbean colony to overturn an anti-sodomy law, and the Human Dignity Trust carries the case in its documentation of constitutional challenges to such statutes.

Entry rules are a separate matter. Section 5(1)(e) of Belize's Immigration Act lists "any prostitute or homosexual" among prohibited immigrants. Jamaican activist Maurice Tomlinson challenged that provision in 2013, was granted leave by the Caribbean Court of Justice in May 2014, and was joined by CARICOM as an interested party in October 2014; on 10 June 2016 the Court dismissed his case, finding no violation of his freedom of movement. Belize argued in that litigation that Section 5(1) applies only to people offering sexual services for financial gain and is not enforced as a blanket prohibition on homosexual immigrants. The Court's judgment also clarified that neither Belize nor Trinidad and Tobago may bar homosexuals from entering CARICOM states, given treaty obligations under the Treaty of Chaguaramas, notwithstanding domestic laws purporting to ban gay entry.

Hate-motivated offending carries an aggravating penalty. Section 8(1)(c)(i) of the Alternative Sentencing Act 2024, effective 27 April 2024, makes bias, prejudice or hate based on sexual orientation an aggravating circumstance in sentencing, and the Anti-Sexual Harassment Act 2024 expressly provides prevention and protection from sexual harassment regardless of sexual preference and gender identity.

Official posture toward LGBT people has been contested. After the 2016 ruling the Government said on 17 August 2016 that it would not appeal, then reversed course after meeting religious leaders on 9 September and filed a partial appeal against the declaration that the Constitution bars discrimination based on sexual orientation. Solicitor General Nigel Hawke argued the ruling was judicial overreach in redefining "sex" to include sexual orientation. The Catholic Church withdrew from the appeal in March 2018, leaving the Government as sole appellant. In December 2011 Prime Minister Dean Barrow publicly rejected pressure from President Obama, stating Belize would not change its laws.

Religious bodies organised openly against decriminalisation. The Council of Churches held a "Take a Stand" rally on 3 December 2011 and a "Belize Action/Family Forum" rally on 23 November 2011 at which decriminalisation was described as "an orchestrated plan of demonic darkness". LGBT activists received violence and death threats around the Supreme Court hearings in 2013, and a 1998 protest against a gay cruise docking is cited as evidence of residual public hostility.

Belize accepted 15 of 17 sexual-orientation and gender-identity recommendations in its 2018 Universal Periodic Review, the first CARICOM country to accept that many, pledging legal reform, explicit anti-discrimination legislation, police training and SOGI data collection; two rights-equality recommendations were noted rather than accepted. The same review cycle accepted recommendations on educational campaigns against societal stigma, universal access to HIV treatment for LGBT people, and addressing discrimination, violence and hate crimes, including training police to respond properly to violence, with sponsoring states including Argentina, Australia, Brazil, Chile, France, Germany, Iceland, Ireland, Italy, Mexico, Spain, Ukraine, the United States and Uruguay.

Social climate indicators are mixed. A 2013 UNAIDS survey of 773 Belizeans aged 18 to 64 found 34% accepting and 34% tolerant of homosexuals, among the highest acceptance rates polled in the Caribbean. Belize held its first Pride Week in August 2017 with awareness and acceptance activities hosted throughout the country, and LGBT organisations including UNIBAM have become more visible and active since the August 2016 ruling. Expat reporting holds that gay travellers have long found Belize friendly.
tangentialFactors:
Belize's trajectory sets it apart from its immediate neighbours in two respects. It was the first former British Caribbean colony to strike down an anti-sodomy statute, and in 2018 it became the first CARICOM state to accept that many SOGI recommendations in a Universal Periodic Review, which places its government commitments ahead of the regional average even as several nearby jurisdictions retain colonial-era prohibitions.

The decriminalisation litigation itself was framed by organised religious opposition and by official resistance that outlasted the judgment. The Government's reversal from a no-appeal position to a partial appeal within a month of the 2016 ruling, and its survival as sole appellant after the Catholic Church's March 2018 withdrawal, indicates that the constitutional position has been contested by the executive rather than merely conceded.

The regional treaty layer constrains immigration policy independently of domestic statute. The Caribbean Court of Justice's 10 June 2016 judgment tied Belize's entry powers to obligations under the Treaty of Chaguaramas, which limits how far the Immigration Act's "homosexual" limb can be applied against visitors from the subregion, though the same judgment left the domestic provision on the statute book.

The 1998 gay-cruise protest and the 2011 rally rhetoric are the source inventory's principal evidence of street-level hostility; no incident data on violence against visitors after the 2016 ruling appears in the material reviewed.
localsOnly:
Residents gain enforceable protections from two 2024 statutes. The Anti-Sexual Harassment Act 2024 covers sexual harassment regardless of sexual preference and gender identity, and from 27 April 2024 evidence that an offence was motivated by bias, prejudice or hate based on sexual orientation is an aggravating circumstance in sentencing under the Alternative Sentencing Act 2024.

The constitutional holding of the Orozco litigation, upheld on appeal on 30 December 2019, extends the Constitution's non-discrimination protections to sexual orientation and treats sexual expression as protected expression. That holding is the domestic basis for the anti-discrimination legislation the Government pledged in its 2018 Universal Periodic Review response.

Organised LGBT advocacy is established and public. UNIBAM has operated as the country's advocacy organisation, LGBT groups became markedly more visible and active after the August 2016 ruling, and the first national Pride Week ran in August 2017 with activities hosted throughout the country.

Police conduct is subject to a formal commitment. The 2018 Universal Periodic Review process produced an accepted pledge to train police officials to respond properly to violence affecting LGBT people, alongside commitments on SOGI data collection and on reducing societal stigma through educational campaigns.

The Immigration Act's Section 5(1)(e) remains in force as drafted even after the Tomlinson judgment. Residents returning with a partner, and advocates campaigning on the provision, should note that the statute's wording has not been amended by the courts and that the Government's litigating position reads the limb as confined to prostitution for financial gain.
